content: Dr. John Edward McGinness, PhD, MD, was a pioneering figure in the fields of organic electronics and nanotechnology. He earned a Bachelor of Science in Physics from the University of Houston in 1966, a PhD in Physics from Rice University in 1970, and an MD from the University of Texas Medical School at Houston in 1985. Over the course of his career, he authored approximately 40 research publications, book chapters, and presentations. Dr. McGinness made significant contributions to the modern field of organic electronics. In 1972, while working in the Metallurgy Department at Youngstown State University, he proposed that electronic conduction in melanins (such as polypyrrole, polyaniline, and polyacetylene blacks and their copolymers) was analogous to conduction in amorphous solids like chalcogenide glasses. This concept, originally explored by Neville Mott and others, involved mechanisms such as mobility gaps, phonon-assisted hopping, polarons, and quantum tunneling. His work anticipated the Nobel Prize-winning research of Shirakawa et al. on conduction mechanisms in oxidized polyacetylenes. Dr. McGinness later joined the Physics Department at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, where he investigated the physical properties of melanin as a potential avenue for melanoma treatment. At the time, this area of research was relatively obscure, with few researchers outside of melanoma studies exploring the electronic properties of rigid-backbone polymer blacks. Notably, Dr. McGinness and his colleagues constructed a voltage-controlled switch using melanin as the active element, demonstrating its electronic behavior and providing a proof of concept for his model of electronic conduction in such materials. This work foreshadowed the 2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery and development of conductive polymers, though with key differences. Unlike the Nobel-winning work, which focused on passive high conductivity, Dr. McGinness built an actual device with a high-conductivity ON state. The voltage-controlled switch developed by Dr. McGinness is considered the first identifiable active organic semiconductor device, where current or voltage controls current flow. This device is a precursor to many later developments in organic electronics and is now part of the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of American History collection of early electronic devices. Furthermore, this device demonstrated high metallic conductivity in linear-backbone conductive polymers, a property that was later highlighted in a Nature article for its strikingly large conductivity. Dr. McGinness also contributed to the understanding of free radicals in the action and toxicity of anticancer drugs such as cisplatin, adriamycin, and bleomycin. He was the first to demonstrate that the kidney toxicity of cisplatin involves reactive oxygen species. Some of this work was conducted with Dr. Harry Demopoulos, who was known for his role in resolving the Doris Duke will dispute and as a consultant for Clint Eastwood's Dirty Harry movies. Additionally, Dr. McGinness explored the dielectric spectroscopy of water bound to membranes and the mechanisms of band gaps in melanins. His research extended to the effects of long-term alcohol exposure on cancer development, the protective effects of antioxidants against drug-induced toxicity, and the avoidance of neurotoxicity in lithium-carbamazepine combinations. His work on melanin and its electronic properties remains foundational in the fields of organic electronics and nanotechnology.
